en.title: How can the same answers crown a different AI winner?
en.summary: "Better" always means better under one scoring rule. Keep the answers fixed, change the price of a wrong answer, and the leaderboard winner can flip.

en.title: Can satellites spot a forest fire while it is still small?
en.summary: A hot pixel from space is a clue, not a verdict. Finding small fires takes finer sensors, frequent revisits, and ruling out heat that is not fire.

en.title: Is the top model on the leaderboard the best one for you?
en.summary: A model has a profile, not a rank, and every benchmark has an expiry date. Start from the error you cannot afford, not from the famous name.

en.title: Did AI just reach the hardest problem in mathematics?
en.summary: An AI pushed the proven share of Riemann zeta zeros on the critical line further, and a proof checker verified it. What was proved, what was not, and who checked it.

en.title: If AI sat Iran's Konkur, which university would it get into?
en.summary: Five models sit three years of the Konkur, live: who is fastest, who uses fewer tokens, who scores higher, and what the score could mean for admission (an estimate, with its range).

en.title: Why does Persian cost more tokens for some AI models?
en.summary: Persian text is usually shorter than its English equivalent (median 0.88 of the characters), yet tokenizers split it into 1.21 to 4.61 times as many tokens.

en.title: Five AIs, one chessboard: which one actually plays?
en.summary: Five language models play each other live, with no chess engine to help. Who breaks the rules first, who blunders, and who really plays once the memorised openings run out.

en.title: When they say an AI makes fewer mistakes, what are they not telling you?
en.summary: An error rate means nothing without its numerator and denominator: a model can make fewer mistakes simply by staying silent more often.

en.title: Did AlphaFold get the proteins of salak and Crimean–Congo fever right?
en.summary: The Nobel-winning AI's predicted shapes for a leishmaniasis protein and the Crimean–Congo fever nucleoprotein, checked against experimental structures with our own code: where it is confident, where it is not, and why that is not a cure.

en.title: Can a single document hijack your AI assistant?
en.summary: To a language model, your instructions and a document's text arrive in one stream of words, so a document can give orders. Two defences, and what each one cannot do.

en.title: Did AI out-forecast the hurricane experts?
en.summary: We recompute the 2025 hurricane-forecast errors ourselves from public data: an AI model against the official forecast, lead time by lead time, plus a look at cyclones Gonu and Shaheen.

en.title: If the answer key is wrong, which AI loses?
en.summary: A wrong answer key only takes points from whoever answered correctly. Key errors are not neutral noise; they can change the winner unless the key is audited.

en.title: Did AI really win gold at the Maths Olympiad?
en.summary: AI models claimed gold-level scores at the International Mathematical Olympiad. Who graded their proofs and under what rules, set beside the official results of Iran's team.

en.title: How does Google Maps know when you will arrive?
en.summary: An ETA is not a picture of traffic now; it is a forecast of the traffic you will meet. The key idea: every road segment listens to its neighbours.

en.title: What will the weather be on Damavand's summit tomorrow?
en.summary: Why forecast models disagree about a 5,610-metre summit, how to correct them to the real peak, and a design for a summit weather service for climbers.

en.title: When is the Chalus road actually empty?
en.summary: An hour-by-hour forecast for Iran's most famous weekend road, built from its own traffic counters: weekdays, holidays and Nowruz, a transparent baseline against a small model, and why the jam is the hardest part to predict.

en.title: When should I leave to arrive on time?
en.summary: Why the average travel time is the wrong number for a deadline: skewed trip times, leaving at a high percentile, the cost of being late against early, and a backtest of how often each rule would have made you late.

en.title: Can negative marking make an AI more careful?
en.summary: Negative marking creates a silence line, t = k/(k+1). It only makes an AI more careful if the model actually changes its answers and its confidence is honest.

en.title: What happens when AI learns from AI-written text?
en.summary: If each generation learns only from the previous one, rare things vanish first and everything collapses towards one narrow answer. Keep human data alongside, and in our test it did not happen.

en.title: Can AI find where you are from one photo?
en.summary: Today's models often place an ordinary photo to the city, sometimes to the street, even with the metadata stripped. Hiding clues helps, but not enough.

en.title: Is tomorrow's wind right for paragliding?
en.summary: What a paraglider pilot needs from a forecast near Tehran, why mountain winds and thermals are hard for weather models, and how forecasts compare with what was actually observed.

en.title: We tested it a thousand times. Can we trust it now?
en.summary: How many questions does a fair comparison need? Paired tests, question clusters and the smallest difference a benchmark can actually detect.

en.title: Every number in this table is right. Why does it mislead?
en.summary: A correct table can still mislead through what it chooses to show: subsets, aggregation and selective reporting. How to check before you believe it.

en.title: The ARC puzzle: people solve it — can AI still not?
en.summary: Colour-grid puzzles most people solve in seconds, which stumped strong models for years. You play the same puzzles, see how a model reads a grid as text, and find out what the newest models now score — and at what cost.

en.title: Which AI says "I don't know" at the right time?
en.summary: Our Bluff benchmark measures when models abstain. The method, the data lock and how to read the result; the results themselves come after the run.

en.title: Where did this AI score come from? Check it yourself
en.summary: A refutable result ships the files a reader needs to recompute it. Recompute vs rerun, versions, checksums and a public correction log.

en.title: Erdős problems: did AI discover new maths or find old answers?
en.summary: Headlines said AI solved Erdős problems. Some solutions were genuinely new; some were forgotten answers already in the literature. What 'new' means in mathematics, checked against the public problem database.

en.title: Can we forecast the next solar storm?
en.summary: A storm warning is a probability, not a promise. Warn earlier and you raise more false alarms; we replay real space-weather data to see the trade-off.

en.title: Can you spot a fake review? Can AI?
en.summary: Humans, simple rules and a model try to spot deceptive reviews. The real question is what a false accusation costs, and whether a detector should flag or delete.

en.title: The answer is in the file. Why does the AI still get it wrong?
en.summary: Give the model every document, or retrieve only the relevant page? We separate 'never found it' from 'found it and misread it', and price each correct answer.

en.title: Why did YouTube recommend this video to you?
en.summary: We build a small recommender on public movie ratings and watch two identical users drift apart. What the system optimises decides what you get to see.

en.title: We gave a paper to an AI agent. Can it repeat the experiment?
en.summary: One success is a demo. We run an agent on the same multi-step tasks many times and count how often it finishes every step without breaking anything.

en.title: The AI's form is perfectly tidy. So why is the answer wrong?
en.summary: Valid JSON, a schema that passes, and a wrong amount. We separate three checks (it parses, it fits the form, it is true) and measure which errors slip past each one.

en.title: Does AI treat two identical résumés differently?
en.summary: Same skills, different name. A paired audit of AI résumé screening with synthetic CVs, repeated runs and a name-blind control, and where a human must stay in the loop.

en.title: Do we need the most expensive AI for every question?
en.summary: A small model, a large one, and a router between them. We pick the router's threshold on one set, test it on another, and count the cost of each acceptable answer.

en.title: What happens when a hundred people ask the AI at once?
en.summary: The demo was fast for one person. We load our own AI service with 1, 10, 50 and 100 virtual users and watch the queue, the waiting time and the errors.

en.title: Does AI really work without the internet?
en.summary: We unplug the internet and run fixed Persian and English tasks on a laptop model, then the same tasks on an online model: what still works, how fast, and at what cost.
